steps.premise: Kite string left in grass is hard to spot and can wrap around the mower spindle.
steps.action: Give the mowing crew time to check the grass for kite line before every cut.
steps.consequence: The crew can clear loose line before it catches in the mower.
steps.quote: Give the mower crew a few minutes for a line sweep before each cut. Loose kite string is hard to see in the grass and can wind around a mower spindle.

steps.premise: Repeated launches wear out the same spot.
steps.action: Shift the launch markers a short distance each week.
steps.consequence: Grass can recover where people launched before.
steps.quote: Everyone tends to launch from the same bare patch. Moving the launch flags a little each week gives the grass time to grow back.

steps.premise: Children often watch from beneath the kites.
steps.action: Place a bench to the side where spectators can see well.
steps.consequence: Families can watch comfortably away from the kite lines.
steps.quote: Children like to watch from directly under the kites. A bench with a good view off to one side gives families a comfortable spot clear of the lines.

steps.premise: Walkers cutting across the field can miss a stretched kite line.
steps.action: Mow a walking path along the field boundary.
steps.consequence: Walkers can see a route around the flying area.
steps.quote: People taking a shortcut across the grass may never notice a line stretched in front of them. A mown path around the edge gives walkers an obvious way through.

steps.premise: A visiting school group can occupy the entire field.
steps.action: Post scheduled group visits on the field noticeboard.
steps.consequence: Regular users can plan to fly when the field is quieter.
steps.quote: One school outing can fill the whole field. Listing group visits on the noticeboard lets regular flyers choose a quieter time.

steps.premise: Wind can blow away small clips while people assemble kites.
steps.action: Provide a shallow tray with raised edges on the assembly table.
steps.consequence: The small parts stay together until assembly is complete.
steps.quote: Wind often scatters tiny clips during assembly. A shallow lipped tray on the work table keeps the fittings together until the kite is ready.

steps.premise: Knowing what equipment the room already has helps a quartet set up faster.
steps.action: Display a dated list of the room’s equipment next to the booking form.
steps.consequence: Musicians can decide which equipment they need to bring.
steps.quote: A quartet can set up much faster if it knows what is already in the room. Put a dated equipment list beside the booking form so players can decide what to bring.

steps.premise: Some musicians arrive after rehearsal starts.
steps.action: Include the entry code in the booking message.
steps.consequence: Latecomers can enter without interrupting a piece.
steps.quote: Some players arrive after everyone else has begun. Giving them the door code in the booking message saves the ensemble from stopping mid-piece to let them in.

steps.premise: Musicians make bowing notes during rehearsal.
steps.action: Fit each music stand with a groove or clip for a pencil.
steps.consequence: Players can reach a pencil on their stand.
steps.quote: Put a pencil groove or clip on each music stand. Players mark bowings as they rehearse, and a pencil that stays on the stand is always within reach.

steps.premise: In a small rehearsal room, drums can overpower a flute.
steps.action: Make practice pads available for the drums.
steps.consequence: Mixed ensembles can hear soft parts as they rehearse.
steps.quote: A drum kit can drown a flute in a small room. Stock a set of practice pads so mixed groups can hear the quieter parts while they work through a passage.

steps.premise: An ensemble may change the mixer’s channel levels.
steps.action: Provide a photograph of the usual mixer settings.
steps.consequence: The following group can quickly find a starting setup.
steps.quote: A photo of the mixer's usual settings gives the next ensemble a quick starting point after a group has turned individual channels up or down.

steps.premise: An ensemble may want a freshly tuned piano for a recording.
steps.action: Show the tuner’s visit on the shared calendar.
steps.consequence: The ensemble can schedule its recording soon after the tuning.
steps.quote: Leave the piano tuner's visit on the shared calendar. Ensembles scheduling a recording can pick a date when the instrument will have just been tuned.

steps.premise: Some residents seldom visit the shops.
steps.action: Give residents a box to tick on the signup slip for home delivery.
steps.consequence: Those residents can still get a copy at home.
steps.quote: Ask residents to mark a small box on the signup slip if they prefer a doorstep copy. People who rarely get to the shops would still receive the bulletin.

steps.premise: A bundle that reaches a closed shop has to go around the route again.
steps.action: Agree on a delivery time with each shopkeeper.
steps.consequence: The carrier can leave the bundle on the first visit.
steps.quote: Arrange a delivery time with each shopkeeper. A bundle arriving before the doors open otherwise has to travel around the route a second time.

steps.premise: A reader might move to another address in the neighborhood.
steps.action: Provide a phone number where readers can report an address change.
steps.consequence: Delivery continues at the new home and papers stop piling up at the old one.
steps.quote: Give readers a phone number for address changes. Someone who moves within the neighborhood can keep receiving a copy, and the old doorstep stops accumulating papers.

steps.premise: Shoppers can miss the bulletin rack among promotional leaflets at checkout.
steps.action: Put a sign above the rack saying that copies are free.
steps.consequence: Shoppers have a reason to take a bulletin.
steps.quote: A full rack by the checkout is easy to overlook among the sale leaflets. A small sign above it telling shoppers the bulletin is free gives them a reason to take one.

steps.premise: A holiday closure could block the carrier’s usual way around a street.
steps.action: Mark announced closures on that week’s delivery map.
steps.consequence: The carrier can approach from the other end of the block.
steps.quote: A holiday street closure can cut a carrier off halfway around the block. Note announced closures on the week's route map so the carrier can enter from the other end.

steps.premise: Households may be away for a week.
steps.action: Allow a household to suspend home delivery for the week it chooses.
steps.consequence: Papers will not pile up during its absence.
steps.quote: Let households pause a doorstep delivery for a specified week. They can go away without coming back to a pile of old bulletins.

steps.premise: Some children have trouble gripping a thin puppet stick.
steps.action: Make large loop handles for them to hold.
steps.consequence: They can operate their own puppets independently.
steps.quote: Make a few large loop handles for children who find a narrow stick difficult to hold. They can move their own characters without an adult taking over.

steps.premise: Adults can block the youngest spectators’ view.
steps.action: Give those children floor cushions at the front.
steps.consequence: They can see the entire screen.
steps.quote: Give the youngest audience members cushions on the floor at the front. They can see the whole screen without having to look around adult shoulders.

steps.premise: Sudden darkness can bother some children.
steps.action: Lower the lights gradually and let children know the performance is about to begin.
steps.consequence: Children have time to settle in.
steps.quote: Some children dislike a room going dark all at once. Dim the lights in stages and tell them when the show is about to start so they can settle in.

steps.premise: A child using a wheelchair needs to reach the screen from a seated position.
steps.action: Keep one side of the screen accessible at seated height.
steps.consequence: The child can perform in a scene alongside a standing partner.
steps.quote: Leave a clear approach to one side of the screen at seated height. A child using a wheelchair can bring a puppet into the same scene as a standing partner.

steps.premise: Children operating puppets behind the sheet cannot see the audience’s faces.
steps.action: Have partners switch sides after each short scene.
steps.consequence: Each child can see the puppetry from the audience’s viewpoint.
steps.quote: Children behind the sheet can't see the faces out front. Let pairs trade places after each short scene so they can see how their work looks from the audience.

steps.premise: unspecified
steps.action: Place samples of translucent colored paper beside the puppet shapes for children to hold to the light.
steps.consequence: They can select a color that will be visible on the screen.
steps.quote: Set out a small sample of colored translucent paper beside the silhouettes. Children can hold it up to the light and choose a color that actually shows on the screen.

steps.premise: Stacks of postcards obscure most of the designs.
steps.action: Display an upright example of every design.
steps.consequence: Visitors can choose a familiar view.
steps.quote: A row of card stacks hides most of the pictures. Prop up one of each design so visitors can pick out a view they recognize.

steps.premise: The postage required varies with the destination.
steps.action: Have the volunteer ask where the card is going before giving out a stamp.
steps.consequence: An overseas card gets appropriate postage.
steps.quote: Postage depends on where the card is going, so have the stamp volunteer ask the destination before handing over a stamp. That keeps a card for overseas from leaving with domestic postage.

steps.premise: A child can have a story to tell before learning to write.
steps.action: Have a volunteer write down what the child says.
steps.consequence: The postcard carries the child’s own words.
steps.quote: A child may have a whole story to send before they can form the letters. A volunteer who takes dictation can get the child's own words onto the card.

steps.premise: Some visitors arrive in the afternoon.
steps.action: Set aside several postcard designs for later in the day.
steps.consequence: Later visitors can still choose among pictures.
steps.quote: Keep a few card designs in reserve for the afternoon so late arrivals still have a choice of pictures.

steps.premise: unspecified
steps.action: Use a small ruler as a guide on the writing side, shifting it down for each line.
steps.consequence: The lines of writing stay apart.
steps.quote: A short ruler makes a good line guide on the blank side. Writers can move it down as they go and keep their lines from drifting into each other.

steps.premise: Visitors may deposit cards moments before the table closes.
steps.action: Assign a volunteer to carry the collection box to the post office at closing.
steps.consequence: Someone is responsible for mailing even the last cards.
steps.quote: Name a volunteer to take the collection box to the post office at closing. Cards left in the final few minutes then have someone responsible for getting them into the mail.

steps.premise: Linens returned on Saturday still need laundering.
steps.action: Reserve drying and folding time on the booking calendar.
steps.consequence: Staff can offer Sunday borrowers only the linens they can have ready.
steps.quote: A Saturday return still has to go through the wash. Block out drying and folding time on the booking calendar so Sunday's group is offered only what can be ready.

steps.premise: The caterer’s linens and the hall’s may get washed together.
steps.action: Put a washable identifying mark in a corner of the hall’s cloths.
steps.consequence: The caterer can sort the hall’s cloths from their own.
steps.quote: A washable hall mark in one corner helps a caterer sort the hall's cloths from their own when both sets turn up in the same laundry load.

steps.premise: Guest numbers may increase after invitations have gone out.
steps.action: Give the borrower a deadline for confirming the quantity while staff can still make changes.
steps.consequence: Staff can adjust the linen order to the final count.
steps.quote: A booking for forty guests can grow after invitations go out. Set a date for the borrower to confirm the final quantity while staff still have time to adjust the order.

steps.premise: A fold can hide a stain in an apparently clean pile.
steps.action: Unfold each cloth in bright light before packing it.
steps.consequence: The borrower receives linens fit to put on the tables.
steps.quote: A stack can look spotless while a mark hides inside a fold. Open each tablecloth under a bright light before packing it so the borrower gets a presentable set.

steps.premise: New borrowers may arrive when the main hall is locked.
steps.action: Include a photograph of the collection entrance in the pickup email.
steps.consequence: They can find the linen room directly.
steps.quote: Put a picture of the collection door in the pickup email. First-time borrowers can go straight to the linen room even when the main hall is locked.

steps.premise: A borrower may have tables of several shapes.
steps.action: Bundle linens by room and table number.
steps.consequence: The setup crew can deliver each bundle straight to its table.
steps.quote: When a group's tables have different shapes, pack by room and table number. Its setup crew can take each bundle straight to the right spot.

steps.premise: Routine local noise could drown out birds at the first stop.
steps.action: Check the route at the intended hour several days before the walk.
steps.consequence: The organizer can discover recurring noise before the group visit.
steps.quote: Walk the route at the planned hour a few days ahead. A fountain or a delivery truck that runs every morning might otherwise drown out the first stop.

steps.premise: Leaves may conceal the bird that is singing.
steps.action: Describe the bird’s direction using a clock position relative to a landmark.
steps.consequence: Everyone has a common reference for locating the singer.
steps.quote: A clock-face direction such as “two o'clock from the gate” gives everyone the same reference point when the singer is hidden in leaves.

steps.premise: Some participants need to sit during a long stop.
steps.action: Plan the longest listening stop at a bench.
steps.consequence: Those participants can stay for the full discussion.
steps.quote: Choose a stop with a bench for the longest listening spell. Walkers who need a seat can stay for the whole discussion.

steps.premise: Walkers may become spread out on a narrow trail and some may stop to listen.
steps.action: Ask someone who knows the route to bring up the rear.
steps.consequence: A walker who pauses can find the group again.
steps.quote: The group may stretch out on a narrow path. Ask someone familiar with the route to walk last so a person who pauses to listen can find their way back to the others.

steps.premise: Walkers may disagree about which bird produced a song.
steps.action: Record the song phrase in writing along with the different identifications.
steps.consequence: The group can compare the same evidence with recordings later.
steps.quote: If a likely identification divides the group, write down the phrase and the competing guesses. Walkers can check the same evidence against recordings afterward.

steps.premise: A phone chirp can be mistaken for a bird joining the song.
steps.action: Keep phone ringtones switched off at listening stops.
steps.consequence: Participants can avoid mistaking a phone sound for a bird.
steps.quote: Keep ringtones off during listening stops. An electronic chirp from a pocket can sound remarkably like another bird joining in.

steps.premise: A planner user wants to know how a pen writes on their own pages.
steps.action: Provide room for the visitor to try writing in their planner.
steps.consequence: They can assess how the pen works on that paper.
steps.quote: Someone choosing a pen for a daily planner needs to know how it behaves on those pages. Leave room for them to try a few words in their own planner as well.

steps.premise: A visitor may put down a pen to look at what they wrote.
steps.action: Display the pens in shallow trays with grooves.
steps.consequence: A pen put back in the tray will not roll onto the floor.
steps.quote: Arrange the pens in shallow grooved trays. A visitor can set one down to inspect the writing without having it roll onto the floor.

steps.premise: A fountain pen writes with just its own weight.
steps.action: Show this on scrap paper before passing the pen to a beginner.
steps.consequence: The beginner can write without pressing down hard on the nib.
steps.quote: A fountain pen can make a line under its own weight. Demonstrate that on a scrap before handing it over so a newcomer can start without bearing down on the nib.

steps.premise: A few test loops can conceal a grip that grows tiring.
steps.action: Give visitors room to write an entire paragraph.
steps.consequence: They can judge how the grip feels with longer use.
steps.quote: A couple of ordinary loops can feel comfortable even with a pen that's tiring over time. Offer enough space to write a full paragraph and judge the grip.

steps.premise: A left-handed writer may prefer the leftmost seat at a shared table.
steps.action: Give them that end seat when they want it.
steps.consequence: Their elbow has room to move as they write.
steps.quote: Seat a left-handed writer at the left end of a shared table when they prefer it. Their elbow then has room to move through a line.

steps.premise: Some owners allow their pen caps to be placed on the back during writing.
steps.action: Identify the pens whose owners permit that use.
steps.consequence: Visitors can try the added weight while respecting what each owner allows.
steps.quote: Show which pens the owners are happy to have used with the cap on the back. Visitors can explore how the extra weight feels without guessing what a borrowed pen will tolerate.
